title_en: On the Arrival of the Egyptians
author: Gregory of Nazianzus
addressee: A delegation of Egyptian Christians visiting Gregory, praised as faithful and orthodox
occasion: Gregory welcomes Egyptian visitors who have come to him, praising their orthodoxy and using the occasion to defend the full divinity of the Son and the Holy Spirit against Arian and Sabellian errors.
argument: Gregory greets the Egyptians as fellow orthodox Christians who have brought spiritual nourishment by their faithful confession. He contrasts their true worship of the Triune God with Egypt's old animal and idol cults. He then gives a concise doctrinal statement: one God in three, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, equal in divinity, distinct in persons. He argues that the Son possesses all that the Father has except causation, and the Spirit possesses all that the Son has except sonship. Finally, he urges his hearers to glorify the Trinity with the cherubim, David, John, Luke, and Paul, and warns that to deny the Spirit's divinity is to steal from God and falsify one's baptism.

outline.move: Gregory addresses the Egyptians, praising them for coming eagerly and describing Christ as the true bread from heaven who was once called out of Egypt.

He contrasts Egypt's former animal worship and idol cults with the true faith now proclaimed by Egyptian Christians, describes how the Egyptians were strengthened by dangers and became more zealous for piety, embraces the visitors as his own people through repeated 'my people' declarations, and compares their previous maritime gathering with the present one, finding the present one more beautiful and magnificent.
He praises their orderly piety and introduces a brief doctrinal teaching on the two highest distinctions in reality: creator and creation, with God as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

He argues for the full divinity of the Son and the Spirit, rejecting any view that makes them changeable, servile, or unequal to the Father, warns against blasphemy against the Spirit, and makes a personal, emotional appeal about his own baptism and spiritual welfare, culminating in the 'Give me a second baptism' passage.

He summons biblical witnesses—cherubim, David, John, Luke, and Paul—to support the equal divinity of the three persons, directly attacks present opponents as new embezzlers like Ananias and Sapphira, and closes with a doxology.

cast.name: Gregory of Nazianzus
cast.who: The speaker and author, bishop and theologian, welcoming the Egyptian visitors.

cast.name: Joseph
cast.who: Gregory offers two possible referents: the Old Testament patriarch who stored grain in Egypt, or his successor in throne, word, and grey hair, the 'new Peter'—a contemporary bishop, likely Peter of Alexandria.

cast.name: Peter

cast.name: David
cast.who: Psalmist cited as a witness to seeing light in God's light.

cast.name: John
cast.who: Evangelist, called son of thunder, cited for his high theology of the Word.

cast.name: Luke
cast.who: Evangelist and author of Acts, cited for the Spirit's sovereign work.

cast.name: Paul
cast.who: Apostle cited for his flexible ordering of the three persons to show their equal dignity.

cast.name: Ananias and Sapphira
cast.who: Couple in Acts who lied to the Holy Spirit; Gregory directly addresses a present opponent as ranking with them as 'new embezzlers' who steal deity itself.

scripture: Gregory uses the Septuagint (LXX) for Old Testament quotations and Greek New Testament texts. Psalm numbering follows the LXX. Modern citations should use standard English Bible book names and, where applicable, note LXX Psalm numbering.
uncertain: The exact date of delivery is uncertain; 380 is a common scholarly estimate but not established from the text itself.
The precise identity of the Egyptian visitors and their ecclesiastical rank is not stated in the text.
The identity of the 'new Peter' is not explicitly named in the text; the identification with Peter of Alexandria is a scholarly inference.

_unresolved_facts.claim: The 'new Peter' is a contemporary figure, likely Peter of Alexandria, bishop and martyr, praised as no less in virtue than in name; not the Apostle Peter.
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Καὶ Ἰωσὴφ ὁπότερον βούλει λαμβάνειν, εἴτε τὸν τῆς ἀθανασίας ἐραστὴν, καὶ δημιουργὸν, καὶ ἐπώνυμον· εἴτε τὸν ἐκείνου καὶ θρόνῳ, καὶ λόγῳ, καὶ πολιᾷ διάδοχον, τὸν νέον Πέτρον ἡμῖν, οὐχ ἧττον τὴν ἀρετὴν, ἢ τὴν κλῆσιν
_unresolved_facts.fix: The 'new Peter' is presented as a successor to Joseph (the patriarch) in 'throne, word, and grey hair'—not as a successor to the Apostle Peter. The text says he is 'no less in virtue than in name' (οὐχ ἧττον τὴν ἀρετὴν, ἢ τὴν κλῆσιν), meaning his virtue matches his name, not that he is praised as 'no less in virtue than in name' as a contrast. The identification with Peter of Alexandria remains scholarly inference.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Ananias and Sapphira... Gregory directly addresses a present opponent as ranking with them as 'new embezzlers' who steal deity itself.
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Τί μετὰ Ἀνανίου τάττῃ καὶ Σαπφείρας τῶν καινῶν νοσφιστῶν... ἀλλ' αὐτὴν κλέπτων θεότητα, καὶ ψευδόμενος, οὐκ ἄνθρωπον, ἀλλὰ Θεόν, ὅπερ ἤκουσας;
_unresolved_facts.fix: Gregory uses second-person singular (τάττῃ, κλέπτων, ψευδόμενος, ἤκουσας) to directly address a single opponent, comparing this person to Ananias and Sapphira as 'new embezzlers' (καινῶν νοσφιστῶν). The opponent is addressed as one person stealing deity itself, not as 'ranking with them' as a group.

_unresolved_facts.claim: sections ['2']: He contrasts Egypt's former animal worship and idol cults with the true faith now proclaimed by Egyptian Christians, describes how the Egyptians were strengthened by dangers and became more zealous for piety
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Τοὐναντίον μὲν οὖν ἐῤῥώσθησαν τοῖς κινδύνοις, καὶ φιλοτιμότεροι γεγόνασιν εἰς εὐσέβειαν. Τοιοῦτο γὰρ τὸ παθεῖν ὑπὲρ Χριστοῦ... Τοιοῦτά σου, Αἴγυπτε, τὰ νῦν διηγήματά τε καὶ θαύματα.
_unresolved_facts.fix: The description of being strengthened by dangers and becoming more zealous for piety refers to 'Egypt' personified (σου, Αἴγυπτε) and specifically to the Egyptian fathers/champions mentioned in section 1 (τούτων ὑμεῖς θρέμματα...), not to the present Egyptian visitors themselves. The 'dangers' (κινδύνοις) refer to past persecutions endured by the Egyptian confessors, not the visitors' own experiences.

_unresolved_facts.claim: sections ['2']: embraces the visitors as his own people through repeated 'my people' declarations
_unresolved_facts.fix: The 'my people' (λαός ἐμός) declarations occur in section 2, but the brief should note that Gregory explicitly defines this as 'one of like mind and like doctrine, and a worshipper of the same Trinity' (τὸν ὁμόφρονα καὶ ὁμόδοξον, καὶ παρὰ τῶν αὐτῶν Πατέρων, καὶ τῆς αὐτῆς Τριάδος προσκυνητήν), not merely ethnic or geographic identification.

_unresolved_facts.claim: sections ['4']: culminating in the 'Give me a second baptism' passage
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Δός μοι λουτρὸν δεύτερον, καὶ περὶ τοῦ πρώτου κακῶς ἐννόησον
_unresolved_facts.fix: The phrase is 'Give me a second bath/washing' (λουτρὸν δεύτερον), not 'second baptism' (βάπτισμα). Gregory has been speaking of baptism (βεβάπτισμαι) earlier, but here uses λουτρόν, and the rhetorical point is that if the Spirit is not God, his first washing was based on wrong understanding and he needs another—it's a reductio ad absurdum, not a literal request.

_unresolved_facts.claim: He argues that the Son possesses all that the Father has except causation, and the Spirit possesses all that the Son has except sonship.
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: πάντα ὅσα ἔχει ὁ Πατὴρ, τοῦ Υἱοῦ ἐστι, πλὴν τῆς αἰτίας· πάντα δὲ ὅσα τοῦ Υἱοῦ, καὶ τοῦ Πνεύματος, πλὴν τῆς υἱότητος, καὶ τῶν ὅσα σωματικῶς περὶ αὐτοῦ λέγεται διὰ τὸν ἐμὸν ἄνθρωπον
_unresolved_facts.fix: The Spirit possesses all that the Son has except sonship AND 'the things said bodily about him [the Son] for the sake of my man/humanity' (καὶ τῶν ὅσα σωματικῶς περὶ αὐτοῦ λέγεται διὰ τὸν ἐμὸν ἄνθρωπον). This important qualifier about incarnational language is omitted from the brief.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Joseph... Gregory offers two possible referents: the Old Testament patriarch who stored grain in Egypt, or his successor in throne, word, and grey hair, the 'new Peter'—a contemporary bishop, likely Peter of Alexandria.
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Τοιοῦτος Ἰωσὴφ ὁ ὑμέτερος σιτομέτρης, ταυτὸν δὲ εἰπεῖν καὶ ἡμέτερος, ὃς καὶ προβλέπειν ᾔδει λιμὸν ὑπὸ σοφίας ὑπερβαλλούσης, καὶ θεραπεύειν λόγοις οἰκονομίας, ταῖς καλαῖς τῶν βοῶν καὶ πίοσι, τὰς αἰσχρὰς καὶ ἀτρόφους ἰώμενος. Καὶ Ἰωσὴφ ὁπότερον βούλει λαμβάνειν...
_unresolved_facts.fix: The first Joseph is explicitly described as 'your grain-measurer' (σιτομέτρης) who foresaw famine and healed with words of economy/dispensation, using the 'beautiful and fat cows' to cure the 'ugly and lean ones'—a clear reference to Pharaoh's dream and Joseph's interpretation. The 'new Peter' is the second Joseph option, successor to the first in 'throne, word, and grey hair.' The brief conflates the two Josephs' descriptions.
